title: Request for Comments Reference Guide
summary: A historical account that categorizes and summarizes RFCs 1 through 999, issued between 1969 and 1987. It cross-references them to show which are current, obsolete or revised. It replaces RFC 999.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a guide to the first thousand memos of the Internet, like a table of contents that also tells you which ones are outdated.

subtitle: A 1987 catalogue of the first 999 RFCs, grouped by topic and summarised one by one.

tldr.problem: By 1987 there were nearly a thousand RFCs, and it was hard to tell which were current, obsolete or revised.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1000 sorts RFC numbers 1 through 999 into twelve topic categories and then lists every RFC in descending order with its author, date, title and a short abstract.
tldr.outcome: It obsoleted RFC 999 and earlier index RFCs, and stands as a historical account of the first years of the series, April 1969 to March 1987.

today: RFC 1000 is a snapshot of the series as of March 1987. It obsoleted RFC 999 and the earlier indexes, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: What the Guide Covers
sections.content:
The RFC Reference Guide is a historical account that categorizes and summarizes Request for Comments numbers 1 through 999, issued between 1969 and 1987. The documents are cross-referenced to show which RFCs are current, obsolete or revised.

It obsoletes RFCs 84, 100, 160, 170, 200, 598, 699, 800, 899 and 999, the earlier summaries and indexes of the series. It has three main parts: a first-hand account of how RFCs began, a list of RFC numbers by category, and a numbered list with abstracts.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a guide to the first thousand notes ever written about the Internet, sorted by topic, with a one-line description of each.

sections.title: The Origins of RFCs
sections.content:
Stephen D. Crocker tells the story in his own words. The procurement of the ARPANET began in the summer of 1968 and called for four IMPs, delivered to UCLA, SRI, UCSB and the University of Utah. BBN won the contract in December 1968. The use of the network was not spelled out in advance, so a meeting of representatives from the sites started a series of exchange meetings.

About a month after a meeting in Utah, the group decided to write down its discussions. Crocker labeled the notes "Request for Comments", with the ground rules that anyone could say anything and that nothing was official. The first IMP arrived at UCLA on Saturday, August 30 and the second went to SRI at the beginning of October. The first protocols covered only Telnet and FTP functions. After direction from Larry Roberts the group designed a symmetric host-host protocol, with an abstract implementation known as the Network Control Program.

Meetings grew from a half dozen people to 50 and 100, and in October 1971 a protocol "fly-off" at MIT had everyone try to log in to everyone else's site. When the 100th RFC was in sight, Peggy Karp took on indexing them.
sections.plainLanguage: A few students building a new network started writing down their ideas. They called the notes "requests for comments" so nobody would think they were official orders, and the notes kept coming.

sections.title: The Twelve Categories
sections.content:
The RFCs are sorted into broad groups and then subdivided by topic. The RFC's own example is that file transfer RFCs are in 5 (Applications) c (File Transfer). The twelve groups are Administrative; ARPANET Host to Host Protocol; Internet Level; Host Level; Application Level; Program Documentation; Network Specific; Measurement; Network Experience and Demonstrations; Site Documentation; Other Standards; and Never Issued.

The core protocols fall in the middle groups. For example, the Internet Protocol is under 3a with 791, 760, ICMP under 3b with 792, 777, UDP under 4a as 768, and TCP under 4b as 793, 761, 675. Telnet is category 5a and its options are 5b. A single RFC can appear in more than one place, such as 817, 816 and 814, which are listed under both Internet Level and TCP.

For readers of this site, RFC 903, A Reverse Address Resolution Protocol, is listed under 7b, Internet Protocol On Networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a library with twelve shelves. Each memo goes on the shelf for its topic, and a few popular ones are on more than one shelf.

sections.title: The List With Abstracts
sections.content:
The last part, "Request for Comments List with Abstracts", runs from 999 down to 001. Each entry gives the RFC number, author, date, title and a short abstract. Entries note relations such as "Obsoleted by RFC 10" for RFC 3, and the list has sub-entries such as 017a.

The abstracts are brief. RFC 903, by Finlayson in June 1984, is described as suggesting a method for workstations to find their protocol address when they know only their hardware address. RFC 4 is described as the Network Timetable, and RFC 1, by Crocker in April 1969, as discussing Host software and the initial experiments on the ARPA Network.

Numbers that were never issued form their own category, 12a, which begins with 014, 026 and 092 and ends with 853.
sections.plainLanguage: After the shelves, there is a long list that gives each memo's number, who wrote it, when, its title and what it says, in a few lines.
